passage: The school van would honk in ten minutes, but Aadhya and Wasim were deep in a game of "house" under the dining table. "I'm the mummy and you're the baby," Aadhya said. Wasim shook his head. "I want to be the papa who cooks." Aadhya thought. "Okay, you cook, I go to office, and the teddy is the baby." They served a pretend dal. When the van honked, Wasim said, "Tomorrow the baby has a birthday."

qa.q: Where were Aadhya and Wasim playing?
qa.a: They were playing "house" under the dining table.

qa.q: Why did Wasim shake his head at Aadhya's first plan?
qa.a: He was unhappy about being the baby and wanted a bigger part as the papa who cooks.

qa.q: What made their negotiation work?
qa.a: Aadhya listened and changed the plan so both had roles they liked, and the teddy became the baby.

qa.q: How might the teddy's role change the game for both children?
qa.a: It gives them someone to care for together, and it lets Wasim plan the next part of their story.

grounding: Two children negotiate roles and storyline in a game of house before the school van arrives.

passage: In the colony stairwell of their Pune building, Vasudha set out leaves and bottle caps on a step. "This is my shop. You come to buy," she told Sonali. Sonali crossed her arms. "I want to be the shopkeeper too." Vasudha looked at her caps. "Then it's a big shop. You sell vegetables, I sell sweets." Sonali nodded, then added, "And at lunch the shop closes." They both pretended to lock a gate.

qa.q: What did Vasudha use to set up her shop?
qa.a: She used leaves and bottle caps on a step.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling when she crossed her arms?
qa.a: She was likely annoyed or left out, wanting to be the shopkeeper rather than only the buyer.

qa.q: How could a parent passing by support their game?
qa.a: They could stop to buy something from the shop, adding to the story without taking it over.

qa.q: What would change if Vasudha had refused to share the shop?
qa.a: Sonali might have walked off and the game would end, instead of growing with her idea about lunchtime.

grounding: Two girls in an Indian city negotiate roles and add to a shared pretend shop story.

"I'm the Amma. You be the Appa, Rajni."
"No, I'm the Amma too. Two Ammas."
"Two Ammas? Okay. Then who makes the food?"
"You make rice. I make chutney."
"And the baby is crying!" Urmila picked up the doll.
"She is hungry," said Rajni. "Give her milk."
"She's sleeping now. Shh."
"Now we go to the temple, and the baby comes too."
They tucked the doll into a dupatta sling and marched to the door.

qa.q: What food did Rajni say she would make?
qa.a: She said she would make chutney.

qa.q: Why does Rajni want to be an Amma too?
qa.a: Rajni is eager for the important Amma role rather than the Appa part, so Rajni suggests having two Ammas.

qa.q: How did the girls keep the game going smoothly?
qa.a: They agreed quickly on two Ammas and split the cooking, then kept adding new parts to the story.

qa.q: How might a parent listening see this game?
qa.a: They might enjoy how the girls mix home life into play and settle their own disagreements without help.

passage:
Teacher's note, Reena Ma'am, KG-B
During free play, Mehak and three friends set up 'hospital'. Mehak wanted to be the doctor; so did another girl. They argued, then Mehak said, 'You be doctor today, I'm the nurse who gives medicine.' They used a block as a thermometer and gave the teddy an injection. When one boy just wanted to lie down, they made him the sleeping patient. 😊

qa.q: What did the children use as a thermometer?
qa.a: They used a block as a thermometer.

qa.q: Why might Mehak have offered to be the nurse?
qa.a: She seemed to want the game to go on more than she wanted to win the argument, so she found a role she could enjoy.

qa.q: How could Reena Ma'am build on this kind of play?
qa.a: She could add simple props like a toy stethoscope and let children keep negotiating roles themselves.

qa.q: How might the boy who wanted to lie down feel about being made the patient?
qa.a: He probably felt included and happy, since the group found a role that fit what he wanted.

grounding: Illustrates children in shared role-play negotiating roles and a storyline, noted by a teacher.

passage: Under the neem tree in the village, Zubin lined up four stools. 'This is the bus. I'm the conductor!' Zeenat climbed on the front stool. 'I'm the driver.' 'No, the driver is Chotu.' 'Then I'm the lady going to the market.' She picked up a basket of onions. Zubin punched her 'ticket', a leaf. 'Next stop, temple!' Zeenat got off and came back, buying a new leaf-ticket.

qa.q: What did Zubin use as a ticket?
qa.a: Zubin used a leaf as a ticket.

qa.q: What does Zeenat choosing a new role show about how she felt?
qa.a: It shows she cared more about staying in the game than about being the driver, so she happily took another part.

qa.q: What could an older child nearby do to help if the roles caused a fight?
qa.a: They could suggest taking turns at being the driver, so everyone gets the role they want.

qa.q: How might Chotu see being picked as driver?
qa.a: Chotu may feel proud and part of the game, since the others gave Chotu an important role.

grounding: Shows village children negotiating roles and a shared storyline in pretend play.

passage: In a London flat after school, Hiroshi and his friend Jamal, both five, turned the coffee table into a restaurant. "I'm the chef," said Hiroshi. "No, I'm chef," said Jamal. They stared at each other. "You can be chef today," Hiroshi said slowly, "and I'm the waiter, and tomorrow we swap." Jamal agreed. Hiroshi took orders from two teddies on a notepad, and Jamal served invisible noodles in paper bowls.

qa.q: What did Hiroshi and Jamal turn the coffee table into?
qa.a: A restaurant.

qa.q: Why did Hiroshi speak slowly when he suggested swapping?
qa.a: He was thinking it through, torn between wanting to be chef and wanting the game to carry on.

qa.q: What could a parent do to support this kind of play?
qa.a: Offer props like paper bowls and a notepad, and let the children sort out the roles themselves.

qa.q: How might Jamal feel about Hiroshi's offer?
qa.a: Pleased and relieved to be chef, and more willing to be the waiter tomorrow.

grounding: Shows two young children negotiating roles in a pretend restaurant so the story can continue.

passage: At the preschool's pretend clinic corner, Vishal, five, put on the toy stethoscope. "I'm the doctor." Siddharth lay on the mat. "I have a tummy ache." "No, you broke your leg," said Vishal. "Tummy ache," said Siddharth firmly. Vishal paused. "Okay. You have a tummy ache and a broken leg." Siddharth laughed. "Okay!" Vishal bandaged his leg with a scarf and listened to his tummy.

qa.q: What did Vishal put on?
qa.a: The toy stethoscope.

qa.q: What does Vishal's pause suggest before he changed the story?
qa.a: He was working out how to keep his idea and Siddharth's, maybe feeling torn about giving up the broken leg.

qa.q: How could a teacher support play like this?
qa.a: Stay nearby and let them bargain, stepping in only if one child keeps overruling the other.

qa.q: If you were Siddharth, how would you feel about Vishal's compromise?
qa.a: Pleased and listened to, since the tummy ache stayed in the story.

grounding: Shows young children bargaining over the story in a pretend clinic until both ideas fit.

passage: I'm Manoj, Eshaan's uncle. Last weekend Eshaan, who is six, and his cousins lined up chairs in the hall and turned them into a train to Goa. Eshaan wanted to be the driver, but so did his cousin. They argued for a minute, then Eshaan said, "You drive, I'm the ticket checker." He walked up and down, punching pretend tickets. Later he announced, "Next station, beach!" and everyone climbed off. I can't say how much it bothered him, but he kept playing.

qa.q: Where was the pretend train going?
qa.a: To Goa.

qa.q: What might Eshaan have felt when he gave up being the driver?
qa.a: Maybe a little disappointed, but he seemed content in his new role since he kept playing happily.

qa.q: What small step could Manoj take to make role swaps fairer?
qa.a: Suggest a turn system, so Eshaan gets to drive next time.

qa.q: How does Manoj see the argument over the driver?
qa.a: Manoj notices it passed quickly and that Eshaan found another role, but doesn't claim to know Eshaan's feelings.

grounding: Shows young cousins negotiating roles in a pretend train journey, seen by an uncle.

passage:
Monday. Madhuri and Ayesha, both five, start playing house in the school corner. Both want to be the mother. They shout, and the game ends.
Wednesday. Madhuri says, "You be mother today, I'll be the doctor who visits." Ayesha agrees. The doll gets a pretend fever, and the doctor gives it "medicine" from a bottle cap.
Friday. They decide together before starting: "Today there are two mothers and a baby having a birthday." The whole corner becomes a party.

qa.q: What happened on Monday?
qa.a: Both wanted to be the mother, they shouted, and the game ended.

qa.q: How might Madhuri have felt when the game ended on Monday?
qa.a: Madhuri probably felt frustrated and disappointed that the game fell apart.

qa.q: What changed that let the play work by Friday?
qa.a: They took turns with roles and agreed on the story together before starting.

qa.q: How might Ayesha feel when Madhuri offers her the mother role?
qa.a: Ayesha probably felt pleased and more willing to play, since her wish was respected.

grounding: Over a week, two five-year-olds learn to negotiate roles and story in pretend play.

passage: The monsoon storm knocked out the power in their Mangaluru house just after dinner, and the fan stopped. Nirmala, six, and her brother Omkar, four, couldn't watch TV, so they lined up chairs. "This is the bus to Nani's house!" Nirmala announced. "I'm the driver." "No, me!" Omkar sulked. Nirmala thought. "You drive, I'm the conductor. Ticket, please!" Omkar grinned and turned a steel plate like a wheel. By candlelight, the bus stopped at five pretend towns.

qa.q: What did Omkar use as a steering wheel?
qa.a: A steel plate.

qa.q: What might Nirmala have felt when Omkar sulked?
qa.a: Nirmala probably felt a little annoyed, then thoughtful, wanting the game to continue.

qa.q: How did Nirmala keep the pretend game going?
qa.a: She gave Omkar the driver's role and took the conductor's, so both had an important part.

qa.q: How might Omkar feel turning the steel plate like a wheel?
qa.a: Omkar would feel happy and proud, finally driving the pretend bus.

grounding: During a monsoon power cut, two siblings negotiate roles in a pretend bus game.

passage: On a hot May afternoon in their Bengaluru building, Hafsa and Charu, both five, set up a pretend kulfi shop on the stairs, with leaves for money. "I'm the kulfi man," Charu said. "You buy." Hafsa counted leaves. "Two mango." "Mango finished! Only pista." "But I want mango!" Charu thought. "Okay, tomorrow mango comes. Today pista is free." Hafsa grinned and took an imaginary kulfi, licking it loudly. Then they swapped: Hafsa sold, Charu bought.

qa.q: What did they use as money?
qa.a: Leaves.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling when she said 'But I want mango!'?
qa.a: Hafsa felt disappointed and a bit annoyed that the pretend mango was finished.

qa.q: How did the children keep their story going?
qa.a: Charu changed the story with 'tomorrow mango comes, today pista is free', and they took turns as seller and buyer.

qa.q: How might Charu feel when Hafsa licks the imaginary kulfi loudly?
qa.a: Charu probably felt pleased and amused that the idea worked.

grounding: On a hot summer afternoon, two five-year-olds negotiate a pretend kulfi-shop story.

Darshan and Gurleen played "wedding" in the doll corner today. Gurleen wanted to be the bride; Darshan wanted to be the band.

They argued about who would be the pandit. Gurleen said, "The teddy can be the pandit." Darshan agreed and banged a tin drum for the baraat.

On Pongal in the village near Madurai, Sumit and Lavanya, both five, played house in the cowshed corner.

"I'm the amma. You go to the fields," Lavanya said.

"I want to cook the pongal!" Sumit said.

Lavanya thought. "Okay, you cook. I'll decorate the cows."

Sumit stirred sand in a coconut shell. Lavanya put marigolds on the calf's horns.

"Pongalo Pongal!" they shouted.

qa.a: He stirred sand in a coconut shell.

qa.q: How did Sumit feel when Lavanya said he should go to the fields?

qa.q: What helped Lavanya and Sumit agree on their story?

qa.a: Lavanya likely felt happy and proud, joining the festival in her pretend game.

passage: On a dark December afternoon in Uppsala, Oskar and Astrid played "bakery" under the kitchen table. "I'm the baker and you're the customer," Astrid said. Oskar shook his head. "No, we're both bakers, and Teddy is the customer." Astrid thought, then nodded. "But I make the saffron buns." "Then I make the ginger biscuits." They sold Teddy six pretend buns for three pebbles. When Teddy "forgot" to pay, Oskar made him wash the dishes, and Astrid laughed so hard she bumped her head.

qa.q: How many pretend buns did they sell Teddy?
qa.a: They sold Teddy six pretend buns for three pebbles.

qa.q: What was Astrid thinking when she paused before nodding?
qa.a: She was weighing Oskar's idea and felt happy to share the baker role, as long as she kept the saffron buns.

qa.q: What helped the two keep their pretend game going?
qa.a: Each suggested changes and gave a little, so they built one story they both liked instead of arguing.

qa.q: What would change if Astrid had refused to share the baker role?
qa.a: Oskar might have sulked or walked off, and the shared bakery story could have ended in a quarrel.

grounding: Shows two young children negotiating roles and plot in a shared pretend bakery game.
